mean: understanding a plan or situation in the same way
ex: Before the client call, let's make sure the whole Hyderabad team is on the same page about pricing.
with: get everyone on the same page
note: Fine at work; very common in meetings, a little cliché in formal writing. It means shared understanding, not always full agreement.
ex2: Before the wedding, both families sat down to get on the same page about the guest list and the menu.

mean: to say or do something that helps strangers relax and start talking
ex: At hostel orientation, Rohan tried to break the ice by asking everyone which home food they missed most.
note: Casual and fine at work. An 'icebreaker' is a game or question used for this at workshops.
ex2: At the gram sabha, the new teacher from Kerala tried to break the ice by speaking a few lines of Marathi.

mean: in trouble, usually because of something you did
ex: Kabir landed in hot water with the principal after posting the exam timetable as a meme.
note: Casual; fine in spoken work talk. Used for trouble you caused yourself, not plain bad luck.
ex2: The restaurant found itself in hot water after a customer posted a video of a cockroach in the dal.

mean: very rarely
ex: My brother in Toronto calls once in a blue moon, usually when he needs a document from home.
with: only once in a blue moon
happen once in a blue moon
visit once in a blue moon
note: Casual. Hindi says a rarely seen person has become 'ईद का चाँद'; in English you would say 'We hardly ever see you!'
ex2: Grandpa eats sweets only once in a blue moon, usually when India wins a big match.

mean: to learn how to do something after some practice
ex: Riding a scooter in Guwahati traffic is scary at first, but you'll get the hang of it in a week.
note: Casual but fine at work. Followed by 'it' or a noun or -ing word: 'get the hang of cooking'.
ex2: Making a thin dosa on an iron tawa is tricky, but Neil will get the hang of it soon.

mean: the most important fact, or the final result
ex: We can debate the design all day, but the bottom line is that the app must launch before Diwali.
note: Fine at work; overused in speeches. In business it also means profit, so 'hurt the bottom line' = cut profit.
ex2: Fans can argue about the batting order, but the bottom line is that India lost by six wickets.

mean: not able to decide between two choices or sides
ex: Ritu is still on the fence about taking science or commerce after Class 10.
note: Fine at work. 'Sitting on the fence' can sound critical: avoiding a choice to stay safe. Use 'about' + topic.
ex2: Many voters in the town were still on the fence a week before the municipal election.

mean: an idea that is worth thinking about carefully
ex: The retired judge's talk on fairness gave the law students plenty of food for thought.
note: Fine at work and in writing, but a cliché as an essay ending. No 'a': say 'food for thought', not 'a food for thought'.
ex2: Grandma's question about how much food we waste at weddings gave all of us food for thought.

mean: a situation where the rules are unclear, neither clearly right nor wrong
ex: Whether delivery riders count as employees is still a grey area in labour law.
note: Fine at work and in formal writing. British spelling 'grey'; American 'gray area'.
ex2: Selling home-cooked tiffins from your flat without a licence is a grey area in many housing societies.

mean: a small, visible part of a much bigger problem
ex: The ten fake degree cases caught this year may be just the tip of the iceberg, officials warned.
with: just the tip of the iceberg
only the tip of the iceberg
merely the tip of the iceberg
instead: a small part of a bigger problem
note: Fine at work and in news, but a cliché; use it once. Almost always about problems, rarely good things.
ex2: The leaking tap turned out to be the tip of the iceberg; the whole bathroom pipeline needed changing.

mean: back at the start, because the first attempt failed
ex: The landlord backed out at the last minute, so we're back to square one in our flat hunt in Koramangala.
note: Casual; fine at work. It means the effort so far was wasted and you must start over.
ex2: The tailor stitched the blouse too tight, so Shalini was back to square one two days before the wedding.

mean: to do something cheaply or quickly by skipping important steps
ex: Engineers say the flyover cracked because the contractor chose to cut corners on cement and steel.
note: Fine at work; always critical. Use 'cut corners on' + what was skimped. Not the same as a clever shortcut or jugaad.
ex2: A good cook never tries to cut corners on biryani; the rice needs its full time on dum.

mean: a big, obvious problem that everyone avoids talking about
ex: At the family meeting about Dadi's house, the loan Chacha never repaid was the elephant in the room.
with: address the elephant in the room
ignore the elephant in the room
the elephant in the room is
note: Fine at work, a little overused. 'Let's address the elephant in the room' is a polite way to raise an awkward issue.
ex2: In the review meeting, the founder's habit of changing plans every week was the elephant in the room.

mean: something that has both good and bad effects
ex: Working from home is a double-edged sword: no Gurugram traffic, but the workday never seems to end.
note: Fine at work and in writing; Hindi uses the same picture. A cliché in essays, so don't lean on it.
ex2: Sudden fame can be a double-edged sword for young cricketers from small towns.

mean: someone who argues the other side on purpose to test an idea
ex: Let me play devil's advocate: what if customers in small towns don't want home delivery at all?
note: Fine at work. Usually 'play devil's advocate'. You may not believe the view yourself; you are testing the plan.
ex2: During debate practice, Ms D'Souza played devil's advocate so the students could test their points.

mean: to unfairly change the rules or targets after someone has started
ex: Every time we meet the sales target, the regional head seems to move the goalposts again.
note: Fine at work, but it is a complaint about unfairness. From football. Often 'keep moving the goalposts'.
ex2: Papa promised me a cycle for 85 per cent and then said 90, so please don't move the goalposts again.

mean: to finally do something hard or unpleasant that you have been avoiding
ex: After months of back pain, Sunita decided to bite the bullet and book the surgery.
note: Casual; fine at work. Used for accepting a hard choice, not for bravery in danger.
ex2: With rents rising in Mumbai, the Shaikh family had to bite the bullet and move to Kalyan.

mean: something that seemed bad at first but turned out to be good
ex: Missing the flight to Goa was a blessing in disguise; that evening I met my future business partner.
with: turn out to be a blessing in disguise
instead: bad luck that turned out well
note: Casual and fine at work; a cliché in essays. Said afterwards, once the good side shows. Hindi: 'जो होता है, अच्छे के लिए होता है'.
ex2: Losing the lead role in the school play was a blessing in disguise; Tara found she loved directing.

mean: to understand a hidden meaning that is not said openly
ex: The HR email only says 'restructuring', but read between the lines and you can see layoffs coming.
with: learn to read between the lines
if you read between the lines
note: Fine at work. Careful: you can also 'read in' meanings that were never there.
ex2: When Ma says 'do whatever you like' about the wedding, you have to read between the lines.

mean: an unimportant point that pulls attention away from the real issue
ex: In the meeting on hostel fees, the dress-code question was a red herring that ate up half an hour.
note: Fine at work and in formal writing; common in mystery stories and debates. It misleads, often on purpose.
ex2: In the detective serial, the missing gold necklace was a red herring; the real clue was the train ticket.

mean: the biggest part of something
ex: Bengaluru and Delhi still take the lion's share of startup funding in India.
note: Fine at work and in writing. It means the largest part, not all of it, and often hints the split is unfair.
ex2: Rice and wheat take the lion's share of the canal water in many districts of Punjab.

mean: a trap where you cannot win, because each condition blocks the other
ex: It's a catch-22 for freshers: companies want experience, but you can't get experience without a job.
note: Fine at work and in writing; often written 'Catch-22', after Joseph Heller's 1961 novel. Use it for circular traps, not any hard choice.
ex2: Shabnam faced a catch-22: the bank wanted proof of address, and the landlord wanted a bank account first.

mean: to stop trying because you are happy with past success
ex: Topping the district in Class 10 is great, Aditi, but don't rest on your laurels in Class 11.
note: Fine at work and in writing. Change 'your' to fit: our, their, its. Laurels were the leaf crowns given to winners in ancient Greece.
ex2: 'Never rest on your laurels,' the old coach told the junior football team after their big win in Kolkata.

mean: a win that cost so much that it was hardly worth winning
ex: Winning the boundary case after twelve years and lakhs in fees was a pyrrhic victory for the Shetty brothers.
note: Formal writing and news. Often capitalised 'Pyrrhic', after King Pyrrhus, who beat Rome but lost much of his army. Say PIR-ik.
ex2: Winning the argument at Diwali dinner was a pyrrhic victory; my cousin did not speak to me for months.

mean: a so-called choice where you must take the one thing offered or nothing
ex: With only one bus to the village after 6 pm, it was Hobson's choice: squeeze into the 6:10 or walk home.
note: Formal and a bit old-fashioned. Not a hard choice between two options (that is a dilemma); it is no real choice at all.
ex2: With only one hospital within fifty kilometres, villagers face Hobson's choice when someone falls ill.

mean: the idea that the simplest explanation that fits the facts is usually right
ex: The fan stopped and so did the fridge; by Occam's razor, it's a power cut, not two broken machines.
note: Formal and academic. A rule of thumb, not proof. Named after William of Ockham, a 14th-century English friar.
ex2: The doctor used Occam's razor: one infection explained the fever, cough and rash better than three separate illnesses.

mean: something very easy to do
ex: After months of practice, the driving test at the Pune RTO was a piece of cake for Shruti.
with: it was a piece of cake
not exactly a piece of cake
note: Casual. Fine with friends and in light office chat; avoid it in formal writing.
ex2: Grandpa says making round rotis is a piece of cake, but mine still come out shaped like clouds.

mean: to stop working for now, or to stop doing something for good
ex: It's past nine in the Whitefield office, so let's call it a day and fix the bug tomorrow.
with: decide to call it a day
note: Casual and fine at work. 'Call it a night' is used late in the evening.
ex2: After twenty years of selling chai outside Howrah station, Bapi Da decided to call it a day and go home.

mean: slightly ill; not feeling well
ex: Riya is a bit under the weather after the monsoon trek, so she will join the call from home.
note: Casual and polite at work. Use it for a mild illness, not for something serious.
ex2: Dadaji felt under the weather after the wedding feast, so he skipped his morning walk in Lodhi Garden.

mean: to avoid saying the main thing directly
ex: Don't beat around the bush, Vikram; just tell me whether the bank approved the loan or not.
with: no point beating around the bush
note: Casual, and fine at work. British English also says 'beat about the bush'.
ex2: When the reporter asked about the delayed hospital building, the official began to beat around the bush.

mean: something that has only a small chance of success
ex: Getting into IIT Bombay with this rank is a long shot, but Kavya still wants to try.
with: a bit of a long shot
note: Casual and fine at work. 'Not by a long shot' means 'not at all'.
ex2: Finding a cheap two-bedroom flat in Bandra is a long shot, but the broker promised to keep looking.

w: hit the nail on the head
say: hit thuh nayl on thuh HED
mean: to describe exactly what is causing a problem
ex: When Ayesha said customers leave because delivery is slow, she hit the nail on the head.
with: you've hit the nail on the head
really hit the nail on the head
hit the nail on the head again
note: Fine at work and in speech; a little worn in formal writing.
ex2: The farmer at the panchayat meeting hit the nail on the head: canal water never reaches the last fields.

mean: the final small problem that makes you lose your patience
ex: Three late payments were bad enough, but the bounced cheque was the last straw for the landlord.
with: proved to be the last straw
note: Fine at work and in speech. 'The final straw' means the same. It comes from the straw that broke the camel's back.
ex2: Power cuts were annoying, but the burst water tank during the board exams was the last straw for the Mehtas.

mean: a shock that makes people see a problem and act on it
ex: The heart attack at forty-five was a wake-up call for Ramesh to start walking every day.
note: Fine at work and in the news. Overused in editorials, so save it for a real shock.
ex2: The Chennai floods were a wake-up call for planners who had allowed building over lakes and drains.

mean: to join something only because it has become popular
ex: Every café in Indiranagar wants to jump on the bandwagon and add matcha to its menu.
with: quick to jump on the bandwagon
note: Casual, and fine at work; usually a little critical. People also say 'climb on the bandwagon'.
ex2: When millets became fashionable, packaged-food brands rushed to jump on the bandwagon with ragi cookies.

mean: a fair situation where everyone has the same chance
ex: Small kirana stores want a level playing field with big online sellers who give deep discounts.
note: Fine at work and in formal writing; very common in business and policy news.
ex2: Free coaching for village students aims to give them a level playing field in the entrance exams.

mean: clear signs that something bad will soon happen
ex: When the two biggest clients left, the staff at the Noida firm could see the writing on the wall.
with: see the writing on the wall
read the writing on the wall
ignore the writing on the wall
note: Fine at work and in the news. It always points to something bad, such as failure or job losses.
ex2: When the old cinema hall cut down to two shows a day, the owner saw the writing on the wall.

mean: a situation that creates many new problems once you start dealing with it
ex: Asking about the old land records would open a can of worms that the whole family wants to avoid.
note: Casual, and fine at work. Almost always used with 'open': 'that would open a can of worms'.
ex2: The audit of hostel funds opened a can of worms nobody in the college office had expected.

mean: the one weak point of a strong person or thing
ex: The young opener scores freely, but the short ball has always been his Achilles' heel.
note: Fine at work and in writing. From the Greek hero Achilles, who could be hurt only in his heel. Keep the apostrophe after the s.
ex2: Slow customer service is the Achilles' heel of many fast-growing Indian startups.

mean: a time when several bad things happen together and make things much worse
ex: A weak monsoon, costly diesel and low onion prices created a perfect storm for farmers in Nashik.
note: Fine at work and in the news, though journalists overuse it.
ex2: Exam week, a sick baby and a broken geyser made a perfect storm for Neha and her husband.

mean: a deal that gives you what you want now but costs something precious later
ex: For the young reporter, writing paid praise for the factory owner was a Faustian bargain: easy money, lost trust.
instead: a deal that costs too much
note: Formal writing. From the German legend of Faust, who sold his soul to the devil for knowledge and power.
ex2: Some villagers near the mine call the new road a Faustian bargain, since it brought jobs but spoiled the river.

mean: a danger that could strike at any moment and keeps you worried
ex: The pending court case hung like the sword of Damocles over the small family business.
with: hang like the sword of Damocles
live under the sword of Damocles
note: Formal writing and news; Indian papers love it. From a Greek story of a sword hanging by one hair over a man.
ex2: For Sameer, the bank's recovery notice was the sword of Damocles hanging over every family dinner.
